newsitem.title: POLAND: Pope, returning home, voices concern for Poland.
newsitem.headline: Pope, returning home, voices concern for Poland.

text.p: Pope John Paul ll began a nostalgic 11-day trip to Poland on Saturday, saying that while he was deeply moved to be home, he was worried about some recent changes in the country including liberalised abortion.
"Every time I return home, I am deeply touched," the 77-year-old pontiff, who has had a series of health problems, said at a rain-swept airport in Wroclaw, southern Poland.

"Every return to Poland is like a return under the roof of the parental home, where every little object reminds me of what is closest and dearest," said the Pope, standing with head bowed and his left arm shaking in what is widely believed to be a sympton of Parkinson's disease.
Speaking briefly to reporters aboard his plane the Pope seemed in good form, joking about the rain awaiting him.
Asked if he was disillusioned by some recent changes in his homeland he said: "Yes, certainly, from better to worse."
Greeting him at the airport, Poland's ex-communist President Aleksander Kwasniewski issued a plea to help build bridges rather than walls between political opponents.

The Pope congratulated Poles for their economic, social and political achievements since the 1989 fall of communism and noted an infusion of optimism in the country as it went about the hard task of "learning about democracy."
Poland's economic growth is among the fastest in the former East Bloc and it is advancing towards its goals of joining Western structures including NATO and the European Union.
But passions rage over issues often linked with religion's role, as campaigns start for elections due in September.
The Pope said in his address he could not hide his concern over "problems and tensions that are at times very painful."

"(These) must be resolved through a common and caring effort by all, in respect of the rights of each person, and especially the most defenceless and weak," he added in what Vatican spokesman Jaoquin Navarro-Walls said was a reference to abortion, now the topic of fierce debate in Poland.

The pro-Catholic, trade union-led Solidarity Election Action (AWS) is hoping to supplant the secularist ex-communists now in government at the parliamentary polls and its members hope the Pope's visit will help its chances.
Ex-communists in parliament have stalled a concordat treaty with the Vatican and backed a new constitution, narrowly approved in May 25 referendum, which was opposed by the Church.
Poland's Primate, Cardinal Jozef Glemp last week attacked Poland's rulers saying that many had been reared in a spirit of Marxism and found spiritual values repugnant.
Most crucially, last year the ex-communists and some other parties eased the abortion law, a move which has just been challenged by a Polish Constitutional court.
Kwasniewski, asked the Pope to help cool emotions.

"We Poles today need bridges bringing us together and not the building of walls which divide us" he said, quoting the Pope's own words that even the most complex questions could be solved by dialogue and solidarity without seeking to destroy the antagonist or blurring differences of views.
Kwasniewski, now a social democrat, paid tribute to the Pope's role in the struggle that restored democracy in 1989.
"Let this be said clearly, there would have been no such change without Your Holiness and the Catholic Church in Poland," Kwasniewski said in his greeting statement.

As the Pope drove to Wroclaw's cathedral, crowds of tens of thousands and windows festooned with flags, portraits and flowers in Vatican and Polish colours testified to the Pope's great popularity among his compatriots.

He was to meet Kwasniewski later and celebrate a mass on Sunday in Wroclaw, where an International Eucharistic Congress was ending, then travel to 11 other centres of the West and South in his seventh return home since his 1978 election.
Vatican officials say the Pope knows each visit to Poland may be his last, and the most poignant moment may be his visit to Krakow where he was Cardinal and where his parents are buried.
